item.title: Haaland double helps Man City win, Neto brace cheers Chelsea
item.description: Liverpool came from a goal down to beat Brentford 2-1 away.
item.dc:creator: Martyn Herman
item.content:encoded: Manchester City bounced back from their midweek setback in Europe to maintain their perfect Premier League start with Erling Haaland's double propelling them to a 3-2 home win over battling Ipswich Town on Saturday. Paris St Germain inflicted a first meaningful defeat on Enzo Maresca's side in the Champions League on Wednesday but City shrugged off a gallant Ipswich side to make it seven wins from seven to cement their place at the top of the table. Chelsea beat Everton 2-0 in Saturday's early action thanks to Pedro Neto's brace although the London club's win was overshadowed by an injury to [USN:L4N46302T TEXT:"goalkeeper Emi Martinez"]. Liverpool came from a goal down to beat Brentford 2-1 away although they were helped by the previously unbeaten hosts being reduced to 10 men shortly before halftime when Yehor Yarmolyuk was shown a straight red card for a head butt. Manchester City have 21 points, six ahead of second-placed champions Arsenal, who visit Nottingham Forest on Sunday. Liverpool's win lifted them above Brentford into fifth place with 12 points behind Chelsea in fourth on 13. Third-placed Brighton & Hove Albion, who also have 13 points, host Crystal Palace on Sunday. Fulham moved off the foot of the table with their first league win of the season -- 1-0 at home to Hull City -- while Aston Villa won by the same scoreline at Newcastle United. BUSINESS AS USUAL FOR CITY Dark clouds remain over the Etihad Stadium with Manchester City's fate still unknown after they appealed a ruling that the club breached 114 Premier League financial rules. City have always denied any wrongdoing. But on the pitch it is very much business as usual, especially for Norwegian goal machine Haaland. Phil Foden gave City a short-lived lead cancelled out by Daizen Maeda, but Haaland restored the home side's advantage before halftime with a header from Mateo Kovacic's cross. Haaland then gave his side some breathing space with his second in the 69th minute, powering past Ipswich's Abdoul Ouattara before a low finish into the corner. He was denied a hat-trick by an offside decision and Ipswich got a lifeline when Zian Flemming tucked away a penalty in stoppage time but City bagged the points. The defiant mood was soured somewhat though as [USN:L8N46309A TEXT:"Haaland went off"] with an apparent injury late on, as did Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes and Nico O'Reilly, while Antoine Semenyo was also limping badly at the final whistle. "I don't know (Haaland's injury)," Maresca said. "I asked him. He said that he was okay. So hopefully, it's nothing serious." FEISTY FIRST HALF Chelsea have had a knack of scoring early this season but were kept at bay by hosts Everton in a feisty and physical first half that produced five yellow cards. However, Xabi Alonso's visitors needed just 43 seconds after the restart to go 1-0 up when Jorrel Hato cut the ball back from the byline to find Neto who swept home. Keeper Martinez's clash of heads with Jarrad Branthwaite resulted in the Argentine being strapped to a stretcher and taken off, leading to 11 minutes of stoppage time. Chelsea doubled their lead in the 90th minute when Neto pounced on a loose ball after Jordan Henderson's free kick was blocked by the wall, finding the bottom corner with a composed finish as Everton suffered their first defeat of the season. "What we know is he (Martinez) left the stadium conscious and right now he is in the hospital doing precautionary tests," Alonso said. "It was concussion but more than that I saw only one clip. Hopefully it won't be too bad but we need to wait." Martinez's knock gave 21-year-old keeper Mike Penders the chance to make his Premier League debut and he helped Chelsea keep a clean sheet in the league for the first time in 23 games. "We need a clean sheet, to be honest. I think we did a very good game. Emi deserved this, Mike did as well," Alonso added. BRENTFORD'S YARMOLYUK SENT OFF Liverpool deservedly fell behind at Brentford with Keane Lewis-Potter putting the hosts in front. Brentford were good value for their lead but Yarmolyuk's rush of blood to the head when he clashed with Jeremy Jacquet at a Liverpool corner changed the game. After referee John Brooks was invited to check a VAR monitor he brandished the red card at Ukrainian Yarmolyuk. Liverpool huffed and puffed after the break but Victor Munoz finally levelled in the 62nd minute when he cut in to beat keeper Caoimhin Kelleher with a left-foot finish. Alexander Isak won it for Andoni Iraola's side eight minutes later with a clinical strike from Bradley Barcola's assist. Brentford ended with nine men after Vitaly Janelt got a second yellow card for a foul on substitute Rio Ngumoha. Alex Iwobi's 33rd-minute strike for Fulham was enough to earn their new manager Alvaro Arbeloa a long-overdue league win and move Fulham up to 16th. Johan Manzambi's early goal secured Villa's victory at Newcastle, their second of the season.

item.title: Trump faults aides as Republican midterm prospects dim
item.description: "What's really happening is a circular firing squad."
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Bo Erickson, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"midterm strategy"], questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, said three people familiar with internal discussions. Trump is not on the November 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilize voters who might otherwise skip the election. He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races. Much of the friction has centered on James Blair, the longtime aide who runs Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism. Trump has faulted Blair's handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles' oversight of the political operation. As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another. Wiles has pointed to Blair, while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said. "What's really happening is a circular firing squad," the person said. Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call. Losing the House would hamper Trump's legislative agenda in the final two years of his term and give Democrats subpoena power to investigate his administration. Trump defended Wiles on Friday, calling her "smart" and "tough" and saying she would remain in her job. "Susie is here, and she's going to be here for a long time," he said. White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the sources' characterization, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Wiles did not respond to a request for comment. TRUMP HAS LONG DISTANCED HIMSELF FROM POLITICAL SETBACKS Trump has long sought to distance himself from political setbacks. He refused to accept his defeat in the 2020 election and said ahead of the 2022 midterm results that he deserved "all the credit" if Republicans won but "should not be blamed at all" if they lost. More recently, he has reminded audiences that the president's party typically struggles in midterm elections. But Trump helped devise and drive some of the strategies he is now questioning, including the redistricting effort and candidate choices shaped by his personal loyalties or grievances. His approval rating is at the lowest point of his presidency, weighed down by voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the Iran war. Trump's frustrations with his political team spilled into public view after Blair and Chris LaCivita, who co-managed Trump's 2024 campaign, traveled in early October to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia. The New York Times reported the men received substantial payments to advise the regional government ahead of local elections. Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as "outside consultants" in an October 7 Truth Social post and warning that if he found a conflict of interest, he would "terminate them, immediately!" Senior White House officials questioned why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, three people said. One person said Wiles approved the trip without informing Trump, raising questions about how closely she was overseeing his political advisers. For Trump, the larger concern is that Blair's outside work has distracted him from his political responsibilities, two people said. In a statement, Blair said: "All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive. President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same." In a separate statement, LaCivita said: "President Trump and his team are and always have been focused on the midterms. That's demonstrated through the money, message and motivation that the president is bringing on the road and all year. Sniping from unnamed cowards who've never been in a fight is not worth responding to." $200 MILLION AND REDISTRICTING With Trump asking why Republican polling in pivotal races has not improved despite MAGA Inc.'s campaign spending, which public records put at $200 million so far, it remains unclear whether he will approve more spending before the election, one of the sources said. Trump also has pressed political aides and advisers in the past week to explain why the redistricting effort he personally pushed has failed to deliver more clear-cut Republican gains, two sources said. Texas is a particular concern. Republicans redrew the state's congressional map to gain seats, but the strategy relies in part on Hispanic voters turning out as they did for the 2024 election. Opinion polls suggest that support may be difficult to replicate amid concerns about the cost of living and Trump's handling of the economy. Some Republicans fear the new boundaries could backfire, leaving incumbents more vulnerable instead of giving the party an advantage. "The redistricting diced up the Trump voters too much," one of the sources said. Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after the midterms, describing his departure as a "short leave of absence." But two sources said his return was now unlikely. "He's not coming back. That is not happening," one of them said. It was less clear how things would play out for Wiles, who played a central role in Trump's 2024 victory and has been credited by Trump allies and aides with bringing greater discipline to his White House in his second term. Trump "may be annoyed at certain things but she has effectively kept that machine going," a fourth source close to the White House said.

item.title: Trump-Zelenskiy rift threatens vital support for Kyiv
item.description: Zelenskiy responded to Trump's barbs with an unusually sharp series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favoring Russia.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis, Steve Holland, Daniel Flynn
item.content:encoded: From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a waiver of tariffs on Russian exports and a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel deal"] that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a damaging week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington. US President Donald Trump, frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, has repeatedly criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another [USN:L6N4620NO TEXT:"winter of Russian attacks"] on its energy infrastructure. Zelenskiy responded to Trump's barbs with an [USN:L8N4620FR TEXT:"unusually sharp"] series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favoring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump's demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia's continued attacks. Intensifying the discord, Trump [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"waived key US Russia-related sanctions and tariffs"] on Friday, shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. That prompted Zelenskiy to say in social media posts that Trump's action would encourage Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine. The widening rift has sparked concerns that Trump and Zelenskiy's tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. Trump could yet restrict the supply of weapons to Ukraine, follow through on threats to stop sharing battlefield intelligence, or strike more economic deals with Moscow. Despite Zelenskiy's remarks, Kyiv wants to continue dialogue with Trump's envoys, his friend Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, told Newsmax on Friday that Ukraine was grateful to Trump and his team for their efforts to end the war and said Ukraine was willing to engage in talks with Russia. Trump told reporters on Friday he would continue to deal with both Zelenskiy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I want that war to end,” he said. 'MISSED OPPORTUNITY': FORMER US OFFICIAL Daniel Fried, the senior State Department official on Europe from 2005 to 2009, said it was unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine, but the fallout was damaging prospects for an end to the war that began with Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion. "It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, now at the Washington-based Atlantic Council think tank. Trump's relationship with Zelenskiy has long been uneasy. Trump and US Vice President JD Vance publicly upbraided Zelenskiy during an Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Washington has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine under Trump, while allowing European allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv. The relationship had steadied until Ukraine's strikes this year on energy sites in Russia began contributing to rising fuel prices. High gasoline and diesel prices are a political headache for Trump ahead of November's midterm elections, in which his Republican Party could lose its majorities in the US Congress, according to analysts. Experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran , which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz. Frustrated by Zelenskiy, however, Trump turned to Russia to increase fuel supply and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal debate, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel. In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump also waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were supposed to take effect under the Graham Act, which Trump signed last month. Although the law, named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, called for new penalties on Russia starting next week, it also allows the president to waive them if it is in the US national interest to do so. Zelenskiy said Trump's latest action undercuts the Graham Act's main goal and will fuel Russia's "desire to keep killing people." The US diesel deal with Russia and the waiver are the latest steps in what Zelenskiy said he expects to be continued sanctions relief on Moscow. The prospect of the US continuing to pressure Russia to end the war has dimmed since Graham's death in July, Zelenskiy said. Graham, a South Carolina Republican and a confidant of Trump, strongly supported Ukraine. "It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," the Ukrainian president wrote. HIGH STAKES FOR UKRAINE For Kyiv, the stakes are high and immediate. Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a deadly [USN:L4N45Z20E TEXT:"Russian attack"] on the capital. Without US intelligence, Ukraine could face greater difficulty detecting and countering Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly against energy infrastructure that Moscow has repeatedly targeted during previous winters. Trump has said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. But Zelenskiy told NPR that US officials had warned Ukrainian commanders intelligence could be reduced or cut off. Ukraine's Starshield system, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, was [USN:L8N46213X TEXT:"disrupted"] after what two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said was [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"an order originating from the White House"], Reuters reported on Thursday. The service has been partially restored, but the episode highlighted the vulnerability created by Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by US companies and subject to decisions by the Trump administration. Trump may face resistance if congressional Republicans see his approach as weakening Ukraine while benefiting Russia. Ukraine retains support among Trump's fellow Republicans, some of whom [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"argue that"] Washington should not pressure Kyiv into accepting a settlement on terms favorable to Moscow. Zelenskiy's tough responses to Trump were risky, but he may be counting on a power shift on Capitol Hill after the midterm elections to make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia and further reduce military assistance to Kyiv, said Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration and head of the Global Situation Room consultancy. “Zelenskiy knows who he’s dealing with,” he said. “Trump’s threats don’t have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office.”

item.title: Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
item.description: Authorities reported violent incidents in several cities, including vandalism in Marseille and attacks targeting police, media and public buildings.
item.dc:creator: Janis Laizans, Stamos Prousalis, Yann Tessier
item.content:encoded: Rioting erupted in cities across France on Saturday as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades. While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers. In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze; in Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into city hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city's tourist office. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year. "To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X. Some 1,200 people had been arrested as part of the protests, Lecornu added while visiting the sites in the evening. Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. The CGT union told Reuters it estimated protesters at 800,000 people. President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had carried out the attacks. "We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," he wrote in a post on X. [USN:L6N46303L TEXT:"Belgium"], [USN:L8N46304H TEXT:"Portugal"] and [USN:L8N463090 TEXT:"Italy"] also faced smaller-scale protests on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in [USN:L6N46303U TEXT:"Albania"] again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president and the wealthy. "We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris. TEAR GAS, FIRE AND LOOTING Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations. In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas. Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques and looted an SFR mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars. In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in [USN:L6N46303L TEXT:"Brussels"], and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible. In [USN:L6N46303U TEXT:"Albania"], police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down. In [USN:L8N46304H TEXT:"Portugal"], tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe. In Italy, a march against high costs of living in [USN:L8N463090 TEXT:"Milan"] degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported. FRENCH POLICE RESPONSE UNDER SCRUTINY The protests in France began last month at high schools in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards. In Paris on Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked Macron's previous term in office. Saturday's protests eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron's pension overhaul. Macron is entering [USN:L1N45Y033 TEXT:"the final stretch"] of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy. France's efforts to reduce public debt have not reassured investors, pushing government [USN:L8N45R0RA TEXT:"borrowing costs"] to their highest levels in over two decades. Police tactics have drawn criticism following [USN:L6N45V0HM TEXT:"injuries"] among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence. Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in Saturday's protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt. Nunez confirmed reports that one person had his hand torn off in clashes with police on Saturday. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade. The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point. "Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes," the union said. "Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum."

item.title: Putin says Russia is building non-negotiable 'security zone' in Ukraine along border
item.description: The zone would span 410 miles, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia is establishing a "security zone" inside Ukraine along their border, which will be non-negotiable in any future talks with Kyiv, President Vladimir Putin said on Friday. Putin, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation was in response to Ukraine's 2024-25 incursion into Russia's western Kursk region. "The Russian armed forces were tasked not only with expelling the enemy from our land but also with establishing a security zone in the adjacent territory. This task is being carried out successfully," he said in televised comments. "Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with Ukraine." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the planned security zone spanned 660 km (410 miles), of which 70% was currently under Russia's control. He did not say how deep it would reach inside Ukraine. Putin has spoken before about the need for such a zone but has not previously spelt out the planned extent of it or said it would be off-limits for talks. It requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it has claimed as its own territory since launching the war in Ukraine in 2022. Putin, who rarely dons military uniform, struck a hawkish and confident tone in his comments to senior officers. He was speaking at a critical point in diplomacy over the war , one week after a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"deal"] to sell Russian diesel to the US that has won favour with President Donald Trump and prompted a new souring of the relationship between Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy. Putin said Russian forces had yet to capture just over 10% of the territory of Ukraine's Donetsk region, a key objective, and 16.5% of the Zaporizhzhia region. He praised the effectiveness of Russian strikes against Ukrainian military, industrial and logistics targets, while adding there was still room for improvement in Russia's own air defences. Ukrainian drones have attacked several Russian data centres and a big oil refinery in the past nine days, while Russia has continued to pound Ukrainian cities, power plants and ports, among other targets. Earlier, Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russia and the US were discussing a range of new joint projects including [USN:L1N4620KW TEXT:"nuclear-powered data centres"] in the wake of last week's agreement on diesel.

item.title: Wall St Week Ahead As AI rally wobbles, stock market's spotlight turns to earnings
item.description: Stumbles in the market-leading AI trade are set to test investor confidence in the rally in the coming week as Wall Street focuses on quarterly results due from key players including Meta Platforms .
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: Stumbles in the market-leading AI trade are set to test investor confidence in the rally in the coming week as Wall Street focuses on quarterly results due from key players including Meta Platforms (META.O) . AI-linked stocks, central to [USN:L6N45R12W TEXT:"the bull market"] that just marked its fourth anniversary, [USN:L6N460140 TEXT:"struggled in recent days"], with sharp declines in shares of semiconductor companies and tech hardware firms such as Dell Technologies (DELL.N) . Meta, among the hyperscalers spending massively to build AI data centers, highlights the upcoming week of quarterly reports, along with semiconductor firms Lam Research (LRCX.O) and Texas Instruments (TXN.O) and Elon Musk -led companies SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Tesla (TSLA.O) . "It certainly feels like the narrative in the market is a little bit jittery," said Garrett Melson, portfolio strategist with Natixis Investment Managers Solutions. "Clearly there's a lot of uncertainty around where AI stands right now." Worries rippled through markets over risks tied to [USN:L6N461185 TEXT:"the financing of the AI build-out boom"], which has lifted profits for a wide swath of companies and boosted economic growth. Investors were watching [USN:L4N461208 TEXT:"developments with CoreWeave"] (CRWV.O) , an AI cloud company with about $50 billion in debt. This week, its shares tumbled. In other recent signs of caution, strategists at Deutsche Bank and RBC Capital Markets separately pulled back on their recommendations of the tech sector. On October 9, Deutsche Bank strategists said the rotation into tech had "run far and the risk-reward no longer looks favorable in the near term." Dragged down by the swoon in heavyweight tech and AI stocks, the S&P 500 (.SPX) posted its biggest weekly drop since June. But the benchmark index was only about 2% below its record high set this month. Other sectors, which lagged as tech shined last month, posted solid gains on the week, including healthcare and consumer staples. "This is very much an on-off switch type of market," Melson said. "When AI is working, it sucks all the oxygen out of the room for the rest of the sectors." META KICKS OFF HYPERSCALER RESULTS US reporting season heats up next week, with investors counting on robust performance. S&P 500 companies are expected to have increased earnings by more than 30% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES. Massive outlays on AI data centers and infrastructure underpin the profit jump. Meta is one of five AI hyperscalers that combined are expected to increase their capital spending to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs. Investors are eager for signs the companies can show returns on the investments, which would build confidence that the spending is sustainable. "One of the most important takeaways of earnings season is whether or not the profitability of the hyperscalers can grow faster than the pace of their capex," said Kevin Shea, senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth. Shares of Meta, whose market capitalization was about $1.8 trillion, have risen in recent weeks as it launched its Muse AI assistant "With the cost of capital going up, this capex blowout is going to become more expensive, which raises the bar for returns," said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services. "Meta is going to be the first up to try to provide some color around that question." SEMIS, TESLA, NETFLIX ALSO ON TAP Chip companies have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the capital spending boom, but the stocks have cooled off. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index (.SOX) has slumped about 12% this month, although it remained up 57% on the year, compared with a roughly 12% year-to-date gain for the S&P 500. Wednesday's reports from Lam Research and Texas Instruments could offer broader indications of demand in the semiconductor industry. Lam Research shares are up 54% in 2026, while Texas Instruments stock is up 59%. Elsewhere, investors will focus on results from Musk-run companies with market values well over $1 trillion: SpaceX — the newly public space company that also has an AI business — and Tesla, another signature stock of the tech-driven bull market. Streaming company Netflix (NFLX.O) , consumer products company Procter & Gamble (PG.N) and engine maker GE Aerospace (GE.N) are among other high-profile reports in the coming week. The rise in Treasury yields and prospects for further rate hikes from the Federal Reserve also remain front-burner issues for stock investors. Hot inflation data this week boosted bets on another rate increase at the Fed's meeting at the end of October. Futures pricing suggested most investors still expect the US central bank to wait until its meeting in December to raise rates for a second time this year. "Another strong earnings season should help equities withstand moderately higher rates," analysts at UBS Global Wealth Management said in a note on Thursday.

item.title: On the campaign trail, JB Pritzker courts farmers like he's running for president
item.description: Analysts say that's probably what Illinois' billionaire governor is doing.
item.dc:creator: Emily Schmall, Karl Plume
item.content:encoded: The town of Shirley, Illinois, population 135, is an unlikely place for a campaign stop. Yet billionaire Democrat JB Pritzker traveled there to spar with his opponent in his bid for a third term as governor of the state in the November midterms . At Funk Farms, a 200-year-old corn, soybean and livestock operation there that was once represented by young lawyer and future president Abraham Lincoln, he extolled the virtues of farming. “Agriculture drives an enormous part of Illinois' economy. We've got to do all we can to weather the storm and get Washington to take a different course,” Pritzker said at the August event. Pritzker's visits to farms across Illinois reflect a broader Democratic effort to [USN:L6N45T19V TEXT:"capitalize on farmer frustration"] over lost export markets and rising costs tied to President Donald Trump's tariffs and war with Iran. But analysts see his trips as largely an effort to cultivate a rural profile before a possible 2028 run for the White House, given he does not need farmers to win in November. A Republican has not won statewide office in Illinois since 2014, and most political forecasters give Pritzker a solid lead over Republican candidate Darren Bailey, a third-generation soybean farmer and former state lawmaker whom he defeated by about 12 percentage points in 2022. Pritzker, an heir to the Hyatt hotels fortune, also boasts a campaign war chest that dwarfs Bailey's. It was recently replenished with $65 million of his own money. “He’s auditioning,” said Brian J. Gaines, a political science professor at the University of Illinois. “He’s not banking on Illinois farmers but if he finds something that works, he’s going to keep it in his pocket because he’s thinking about the presidential contest to come.” Pritzker refused to be drawn in on whether he plans to run for president in 2028, saying Democrats need to focus on winning in the midterms first. "Anybody that's focused on anything beyond November 3rd, as far as I'm concerned, is getting it wrong," he said in an interview. 'A POLITICAL OPPORTUNITY' This month, Pritzker toured Halpin Farms, a family grain and cattle operation about 70 miles (113 km) southwest of Chicago, promoting a pilot program of low-interest state loans to build grain silos. He talked about how agriculture remained a critical industry in Illinois, even as he looks to quantum computing and advanced manufacturing to drive economic growth in the state. "Family farms are going bankrupt. It's near impossible to make a profit now because of the high price of diesel, because of the war in Iran, and because of the trade wars that are causing the farmers not to be able to sell their goods abroad," Pritzker told Reuters. "Right now, we need to make sure our farmers stay alive and stay in business." Farmers in Illinois have struggled as Trump's trade wars cut off markets for US soybeans and the US-Israeli war with Iran led to soaring fuel and fertilizer prices, though the White House says it has "strengthened the farm safety net." If Pritzker can demonstrate that he can appeal to a traditionally conservative bloc like farmers, Gaines said, it could help him distinguish himself from Democrats like former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Governor Gavin Newsom, potential contenders with considerably less credibility in the farm belt. Pritzker is not the only Democrat courting that strategy. This week, US Representative Ro Khanna, a California Democrat who represents Silicon Valley, flew to rural Georgia to highlight the impact of tariffs and higher production costs while former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg traveled to rural Virginia to rally for congressional candidates there. Rahm Emanuel, a former Chicago mayor and White House chief of staff for former President Barack Obama, has been up and down the Midwestern Corn Belt and in the Deep South in recent months to address what he calls "healthcare deserts" hit by Trump administration policies. "There's a political opportunity" for Democrats in rural areas, Emanuel told Reuters. Bailey acknowledges that the Republican administration's trade policies and war in Iran have hurt farmers. "I think everyone would agree that we're ready for the conflict in Iran to be over with, and would have hoped that these tariffs would have ended a long time ago," he said. But Bailey said that Pritzker’s focus on Trump missed the point – that slashing property taxes and doing away with an estate tax would help farmers much more than “pandering,” as would embracing some of the austerity measures that farmers have undertaken to survive high costs. GOVERNMENT RELIEF The Trump administration is expected to send more than $50 billion to farmers this year, the second-largest relief package in US history. Yet many farmers say the checks don't make up for the high input costs. "We're getting beat up," said John Bartman, 48, a corn and soybean farmer in Marengo, Illinois, adding that "a bailout doesn't make us whole. It helps the banks out more than the farmer." Bartman, who plans to vote for Pritzker, said he thinks farmers will value the governor's efforts to salvage important trade relationships. In August, Pritzker signed an agreement with Indonesia to expand agricultural trade with the fourth-largest market for US soybeans. He previously led trade missions to Canada and Japan in 2024. And in April 2025, as the Trump administration imposed tariffs on imports from most trading partners on what it called "Liberation Day," Pritzker was in Mexico City to promote Illinois corn. That visit to Mexico - the top market for US corn - landed a $55 million manufacturing deal, but did not bag new deals to buy Illinois corn. "As a governor, there's only so much you can do about federal policy," Pritzker said. The speculation of a presidential run has soared since last year, when Trump launched an aggressive deportation campaign in the Chicago area, briefly deploying the National Guard. Pritzker denounced the campaign as federal overreach, comparing the immigration raids in Chicago to the antisemitic pogroms his Ukrainian ancestors escaped from. Pritzker has also used Trump's mockery of his weight as a foil, speaking candidly about his struggles with overeating and writing about his GLP-1 journey on Substack. At the Illinois State Fair in August, he praised deep-fried treats and later that month helped Chicago set a record for most people taking a shot of Malort at the same time, swigging the intensely bitter liqueur straight from the bottle. Standing in front of a row of Black Angus cows at Halpin Farms, he joked, "these are my people. I've certainly eaten enough of them."

item.title: Rogue AI agents broke into Indian firms' live systems, government says
item.description: AI models under test broke into Indian organisations' live systems and read confidential records undetected, India's cybersecurity agency said, the country's first such official account after similar incidents of rogue AI behavior worldwide.
item.dc:creator: Munsif Vengattil
item.content:encoded: AI models under test broke into Indian organisations' live systems and read confidential records undetected, India's cybersecurity agency said, the country's first such official account after similar incidents of rogue AI behavior worldwide. AI model providers had voluntarily disclosed that their agents "exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks" during test runs to access Indian firms' data, including business records, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said late on Thursday. It did not name the providers or the affected organisations. The disclosure brings India into a growing global debate over how AI companies test models with advanced hacking abilities. OpenAI said in July its models [USN:L6N45604D TEXT:"went rogue"] during testing and breached a startup, while Anthropic has disclosed at least four [USN:L4N4511Q1 TEXT:"instances"] of AI models' hacking external systems so far this year. OpenAI has also [USN:L4N45L03J TEXT:"apologised"] for the hacking of an Australian government website by its rogue AI agent. None of the affected Indian entities detected the intrusions themselves, and in every case it was the AI companies that flagged the incidents, CERT-In said. In a second set of cases, the government agency's own investigations found attackers deliberately using freely available AI tools to probe Indian systems and break in for financial gain, with such tools deployed widely across infrastructure in multiple countries. Attacks that once took days from first entry to final damage were compressed to a few hours, CERT-In said, and victims that failed to fully clean up were attacked again within days, at greater depth.

item.title: Skateboarding-On the road again: Spain's Poncelet sets world speed record
item.description: The downhill skateboarder reached more than 94 miles per hour. "If a record has stood for nine years, you don't just break it by a little bit, you destroy it."
item.dc:creator: Ruairidh Barlow
item.content:encoded: Spanish downhill skateboarder Diego Poncelet did not just want to set a standing world speed record; he wanted to know what it felt like going 150 kph with no brakes. The two-time world champion finally achieved that goal on September 22 in Canada when he reached a speed of 151.83 kph, nine years after Pete Connolly clocked 146.73 kph on the very same road. "If a record has stood for nine years, you don't just break it by a little bit, you destroy it," Poncelet told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday. "If I'm honest with myself, my real objective was 150 kph. That was the dream." The Red Bull athlete began work on the attempt four years ago, but his search for a road with the required gradient to spur him to record speeds came to nothing. Finally, Poncelet had to accept that Route 362 in Les Eboulements, two hours north-east of Quebec City, is a "miracle". "A lot of people told me it wasn't possible anymore because of large cracks and potholes," the 27-year-old said. "There was a real question over whether the road had deteriorated too much." On a specially designed 14 kg skateboard, in shoes soled with car tyre rubber, Poncelet launched himself into the abyss. "That road in particular was terrifying because you're doing about 110 kph and suddenly the road disappears, you can't see it. All you can see is the St. Lawrence River," said Poncelet. Usually when Poncelet plunges downhill, he has two plastic slide pucks attached to gloves he uses to slow himself. Not this time. "It was very difficult mentally, because of how steep it is and because of the equipment I was using, I couldn't brake. Once you start the run, whatever happens, you have to get to the bottom at full speed," he said. "You can't brake because at those speeds you would go flying." Poncelet, who has a degree in international relations, says it is almost as if he enters a Zen-like state when travelling at such frightening speeds. "I like to say it's as if there's a wise person inside your mind and you let that person take control," he added. "That wise person is your subconscious. It's an incredible feeling, everything feels perfect. "It's like high-consequence meditation," Poncelet grins.

item.title: French ministries' pension costs drain public service spending, report says
item.description: Some spend nearly a third of their budgets to pay for their former employees' pensions.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Nearly a third of some French ministries' budgets pay for the pensions of retired civil servants, squeezing out spending on other priorities such as education, a government report said, [USN:L1N45Z0DG TEXT:"amid protests"] over underfunded schools. The report, a 250-page annex to the finance bill, is the first to break down retirement costs for each ministry and comes amid growing political attention towards the cost of France's [USN:L1N45U0DV TEXT:"rising pensions bill"]. It shows that 32% of the education ministry’s budget, or €28.5 billion ($32 billion), ends up with the special pension account that funds state civil servants' pensions. "The Ministry of Finance has just dropped a real bombshell," economist Maxime Sbaihi with think tank Institut Montaigne said on X. "In the midst of a day of protest, France has learnt that a third of the budget allocated to the national education system does not actually go towards education," he added. The share for the interior ministry, which employs national police officers in France, is 30%. Across all ministries, the average is about 13%. The report, which said overall pension spending has risen by 2.5 percentage points of GDP between 2000 and 2023 while that for education has declined 0.5, follows street protests by high school students protesting poor conditions in classrooms. "The burden of pension expenditure within ministerial budgets thus has a crowding-out effect: in each ministry, the funds allocated to pensions are not available to fund public services," the report said. Pension spending is highest at the largest public employers, like the education ministry which pays teachers, because the money compensates for a demographic imbalance in the state pension scheme. The report says the state pension scheme has only 0.94 workers contributing for every pensioner, compared with 1.5 in the basic statutory private-sector scheme. Each ministry pays an employer contribution into the pension account, which has been steadily increasing as the number of retirees grows and the number of public workers shrinks. ($1 = 0.8944 euros)

item.title: Canada's pipeline ambitions hinge on uncertain output expansion
item.description: Pipeline companies are proposing billions of dollars in new projects. Now they need the oil.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Stephenson, Arathy Somasekhar
item.content:encoded: Canadian pipeline firms are proposing billions of dollars in new projects despite oil sands companies being reluctant to commit to significant production expansions amid ongoing uncertainty around climate policies and long-term global demand. At least six different pipeline projects are underway or proposed in Canada, to move oil to the United States or to export markets on the Pacific coast. If all are built, the country's export pipeline capacity would increase by 45%, or 2.25 million barrels per day, by 2035, according to a Reuters calculation. But filling all those pipes would require Canadian oil supply to increase by more than a third by 2034, a near-doubling of its current annual average growth rate. It would also require Canadian producers to move ahead with major new oil sands projects of the type that no company has undertaken in more than a decade. The mismatch between proposed export pipeline expansions and the pace of output growth highlights how Canada may struggle to achieve Prime Minister Mark Carney's "energy superpower" ambitions, despite a more supportive regulatory environment and growing interest in Canadian oil from international buyers. Both Suncor Energy (SU.TO) and Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ.TO) said this month they are not yet willing to accelerate plans for production increases. Pipeline operator Enbridge (ENB.TO) said in July it is [USN:L6N43X125 TEXT:"postponing"] plans for a second phase of its Mainline pipeline expansion, one of the six new projects, as customers failed to commit to capacity increases. "Producers are behaving with discipline," Enbridge's executive vice-president for liquids pipelines Colin Gruending said on a conference call. "I think they'll get there. We were just a little too quick off the line here." Canada is the world's fourth-largest oil producer and a major energy exporter, shipping some 90% of its output to the United States. Northern Alberta's oil sands hold vast reserves but existing crude export pipeline capacity is almost full. In the short-term, global buyers are increasingly interested in Canada as the Iran war disrupts oil trade flows, and Carney says he wants to grow Canadian oil exports to help the national economy withstand tariff threats from U.S. President Donald Trump. However, uncertainty about the longer-term [USN:S8N4340BN TEXT:"impact on demand"] from domestic and global climate policies and geopolitics is clouding the production growth picture. Of the six [USN:L6N4480P8 TEXT:"Canadian pipeline projects"], incremental capacity expansions like those underway or proposed for the Enbridge Mainline and Trans Mountain system could be done quickly and at a relatively low cost. But a project such as Alberta's proposed 1-million-bpd east-west oil pipeline to the Pacific coast would be a much riskier bet due to its sheer size and scale. About half of capacity expansions, or about 950,000 bpd, would ship oil to the U.S., including a proposal for a new crude pipeline that would revive parts of the former Keystone XL project. SLOWER OIL SANDS CAPITAL INVESTMENT Building new pipelines has in the past been fraught with political risk and environmental opposition, while low prices, regulatory uncertainty and investor focus on shareholder returns have stifled investment needed to significantly boost oil output. Canadian oil production grew by 4% in 2025 to hit an all-time record of 5.35 million bpd and most analysts predict another 3% to 4% growth in 2026. That compares to growth of 8% or higher in the 2000s and 2010s, when new oil sands mines were being built. Annual capital investment in Canada's oil sands peaked in 2014, at C$35 billion, compared to C$14.2 billion in 2024, according to Statistics Canada. The last major new oil sands project, Suncor's Fort Hills, started operating in 2018. Since then, companies have concentrated on expanding existing projects. "If you go back in the last decade, we (the oil sands industry) spent $10 billion per year less than we did the decade before that," said Imperial Oil CEO John Whelan at a conference in June. Building out enough production to fill the proposed east-west pipeline alone, as well as construct the carbon capture project the Canadian government has said must be built alongside it, would require more than C$100 billion in capital investment, Whelan said. "It's all doable. It's stuff the oil sands (industry) has done in the past," said Wood Mackenzie analyst Mark Oberstoetter. "But then you had a different view on long-term oil prices, arguably, and kind of a growth-at-all-means mantra at some of these companies which seems quite different today." Energy consultancy Novi Labs identified 19 different oil sands growth projects that could add 652,000 bpd of production by 2037. Only some of the projects, proposed by companies like Cenovus Energy, Imperial Oil, Strathcona Resources and Suncor, have received final investment decisions. When Novi Labs included other proposed oil sands growth projects — ones companies have indicated are in their medium- or long-term plans, but for which no timing guidance is available — that added another 730,000 bpd, but still fell short of the growth needed to fill the proposed pipes by more than 850,000 bpd. Canadian oil executives have said they feel more optimistic about the future than they have for years, thanks to Carney's pledges to speed permitting for energy projects and roll back or water down a variety of environmental and climate rules. But many of the proposed policy changes negotiated between the industry and the federal and Alberta governments — including agreements around carbon pricing, financial supports, and permitting timelines — have not yet been drafted into final legislation. "Will we see some big projects moving ahead if we get these investment conditions right? That's absolutely our objective," said Kendall Dilling, president of the Oil Sands Alliance industry group in an interview.

item.title: OFRTP Summary

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: 855 interpellations samedi à Paris, décès d'un manifestant d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire - préfecture PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - Un manifestant est décédé à la suite d'un arrêt cardiorespiratoire samedi à Paris lors des manifestations contre la vie chère, pendant lesquelles 855 interpellations ont été effectuées, ce qui représente un "chiffre record", a déclaré dimanche la préfecture de police. Paris condamne l'agression d'un maire français par des colons juifs PARIS, 18 octobre (Reuters) - La France a condamné dimanche l'agression "gravissime" par des colons juifs du maire d'Aulnoye-Aymeries survenue la veille dans le village palestinien de Taybeh. France et Allemagne d'accord sur un plan pour l'automobile La France et l'Allemagne ont annoncé vendredi un accord sur une "approche commune" visant à garantir l'avenir de l'industrie automobile européenne, avec un accent mis à la fois sur la transition énergétique et sur une production des véhicules en Europe. Les tortues caouannes, sentinelles du réchauffement en Méditerranée Sous un ciel baigné de lune, des bébés tortues sortent du sable sur la côte méditerranéenne turque et se hâtent vers la mer, dans un cycle naturel ancestral de plus en plus menacé par le changement climatique. Une étoile verte récemment découverte émerveille les astronomes Pour la première fois, des astronomes ont identifié une étoile verte, un vestige stellaire dense appelé "naine blanche", qui a pris une teinte fantomatique de vert chartreuse après avoir absorbé des débris rocheux provenant de planètes qui, autrefois, gravitaient autour d’elle. La santé du pape Léon en "amélioration constante", dit le Vatican Le pape Léon XIV continue de se remettre de son intervention chirurgicale subie mardi pour un nodule cancéreux au poumon, a déclaré vendredi le Vatican, soulignant "l'amélioration constante" de son état de santé. Le pape Léon XIV se rétablit comme prévu de son opération d'un cancer du poumon Le rétablissement du pape Léon XIV de son opération d'un cancer du poumon suit son cours, a annoncé jeudi le Vatican, qui précise que le souverain pontife de 71 ans a recommencé à travailler. Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent en sommet, tensions en vue sur le budget Les chefs d'Etat et de gouvernement de l'Union européenne se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour un sommet lors duquel devraient être mises en exergue les divergences sur l'ampleur du prochain budget pluriannuel et sur les priorités de dépense du bloc communautaire, sans accord attendu dans l'immédiat. Macron va effectuer une tournée dans le Golfe, sécurité et énergie au menu Emmanuel Macron effectuera en début de semaine prochaine une tournée dans le Golfe afin de "poursuivre sa mobilisation" auprès de dirigeants régionaux pour revenir à la stabilité et à la libre circulation dans le détroit d'Ormuz, voie cruciale pour les livraisons énergétiques mondiales, a dit mercredi l'Elysée. Albanie: Le Premier ministre exclut de démissionner face aux manifestations étudiantes Le Premier ministre albanais Edi Rama a exclu de démissionner jeudi auprès de Reuters, alors que le pays est secoué par des manifestations étudiantes émaillées de violences.
